hypotheses.statement: Cerebrolysin added to standardized rehabilitation produces greater motor recovery (FMA-T pattern from T0 to T2) than placebo in subacute ischemic stroke patients with severe motor impairment.

hypotheses.statement: Cerebrolysin preserves ipsilesional motor network functional connectivity and network efficiency relative to placebo.

findings.notes: The printed triple (18, 52, 35.3%) cannot cohere: 18/52 = 34.6% and 19/52 = 36.5%, so 35.3% is not attainable on a denominator of 52. The benign and almost certainly correct reading is a typographical error in the denominator: the paper's own placebo full analysis set is n = 51 throughout (abstract, Results 3.1, Table 1 header), and 18/51 rounds to exactly 35.3%. The adjacent Cerebrolysin figure (25/59 = 42.4%) is correct. This is a transcription error in a Results sentence, not evidence about the underlying data. Flagged at the tool's severity because the numbers as printed are arithmetically incompatible; the editorial stage should present it as a correctable typo. Awaiting the GRIM-family R cross-check held by the editorial stage.

consequence.explanation: The sentence reports descriptive MEP response rates; no significance claim in the paper depends on whether the placebo denominator is 51 or 52.

findings.quote: Of all patients treated with the studied medication (n = 119), a total of 92.4% received 21 infusions (Cerebrolysin 96.7%, placebo 87.9%). Although five patients in the Cerebrolysin group (8.1%) and five in the placebo group (8.3%) suffered from an adverse event
findings.notes: Both percentages are described in the same two sentences as shares of the safety population, which the paper states is n = 119. No arm size at or below 119 makes both attainable. The two figures individually resolve to different denominators: 96.7% is 59/61 and 8.1% is 5/62. Read together with the placebo arm (87.9% = 51/58, 8.3% = 5/60), the infusion percentages imply arm sizes 61 + 58 = 119 (the treated/safety population, consistent with 110/119 = 92.4%), whereas the adverse-event percentages imply 62 + 60 = 122 (the randomized population). The most likely explanation is that adverse-event rates were computed on the randomized denominators while the sentence attributes them to the treated population, contradicting the paper's own definition of the safety population. n_max = 119 is the paper's own stated total, so the empty intersection is a fact about the paper's numbers, not about a range we chose.

consequence.explanation: Affects the safety claim that adverse events were balanced (8.1% vs 8.3%); the denominators used are not the population the sentence names, so the reported rates are not the safety-population rates.

findings.quote: A total of 174 stroke patients were screened. Of these, 122 patients were randomized after excluding 54 patients who did not meet criteria of severe motor impairment (30 patients) or who refused to participate (24 patients).
findings.notes: Randomized plus excluded exceeds the screened total by 2. The exclusion reasons themselves reconcile exactly (30 + 24 = 54), and every subsequent stage of the flow reconciles exactly (122 - 3 = 119 treated; 119 - 9 = 110 FAS; 59 + 51 = 110; 21 + 19 = 40 and 38 + 32 = 70 summing to 110; 102 - 10 = 92 DTI; 92 - 11 = 81 rs-fMRI). So the discrepancy is isolated to the screening line: either 174 should read 176, or 2 patients are unaccounted for between screening and randomization. This was 1 inconsistent row out of 33 sums evaluated in a single batch.

consequence.explanation: No analysis uses the screened total; the analysed samples (110 FAS, 92 DTI, 81 rs-fMRI) all reconcile internally.

findings.quote: ΔFMA-LL	Cerebrolysin	3.3 ± 5.0	4.0 ± 6.0	7.4 ± 6.3
findings.notes: I recomputed all nine Cerebrolysin-vs-placebo comparisons in Table 2 from the printed means, SDs and group sizes, because every unmarked cell carries an implicit 'p >= 0.05' claim under the table's footnote. Eight cells agree with their marking. This one does not: the lower-limb improvement over the treatment period T0-T1 is significant at the conventional 0.05 level under BOTH Welch (p = 0.0329) and Student (p = 0.0305) readings, yet carries no asterisk, while two cells with the asterisk have p = 0.0157 (dFMA-T T1-T2) and p = 0.0239 (dFMA-UL T1-T2). The unmarked significant difference favours PLACEBO (5.6 vs 3.3 points). The other six unmarked cells are comfortably non-significant (p = 0.12 to 0.75). No single threshold reproduces the printed pattern of asterisks: at alpha = 0.05 this cell should be starred, and at the Bonferroni-corrected threshold the paper says it used, the starred dFMA-UL T1-T2 cell (p = 0.0239) should not be. Note the paper does not state which test produced Table 2's markings beyond 'the independent t-test was used between the two groups to analyze the change in motor function'.

consequence.explanation: A significant group difference favouring placebo on lower-limb recovery during the treatment period is left unmarked, while the paper's narrative reports only differences favouring Cerebrolysin.

findings.notes: The tool returned highly_suspicious; I have recorded it as suspicious because that verdict rests on an assumption I supplied rather than one the paper states. RIVETS tests the reported p against what an independent t-test on the printed means and SDs could yield. The paper never says which test produced Table 1's p-values, and lesion volume is severely right-skewed (SD is 1.5x the mean, on a quantity bounded below by zero), so a rank-based test is the natural choice and would legitimately give a different p. The gap is the largest of the three Table 1 misses: reported 0.117 against an achievable two-tailed ceiling of 0.0954. Worth a clarification of which test was used, not an accusation.

consequence.explanation: Supports the claim of no baseline imbalance in lesion volume; under a t-test reading the true p would be nearer 0.09, still non-significant but closer to the threshold given the 26 cm3 raw difference.

Reported 0.882 sits just outside that, by 0.011. findings.location: Table 1, Lesion volume row (Cerebrolysin) against the normality claim in Section 2.5
findings.quote: The Shapiro–Wilk normality test was used to determine whether assessment values showed a normal distribution; all assessment values were found to have a normal distribution (p > 0.05 by the Shapiro–Wilk normality test).
findings.notes: The paper asserts that ALL assessment values were normally distributed by Shapiro-Wilk. For lesion volume that assertion is hard to sustain: a normal distribution with mean 43.9 and SD 66.7 places 25.5% of its mass below zero, and a lesion volume cannot be negative. The tool correctly notes this does not violate a distribution-free bound and that a parametric test needs normality of the sampling distribution of the MEAN, not of the raw values -- so this is a question about the stated normality check, not a reporting error in itself. It matters here mainly because it bears on which test Table 1's lesion-volume p-value came from (see table1_lesion_volume_p).

consequence.explanation: Bears on the blanket methods claim that all values passed Shapiro-Wilk, which in turn justifies the parametric tests used throughout.

source.source_quote: A total of 174 stroke patients were screened. Of these, 122 patients were randomized after excluding 54 patients who did not meet criteria of severe motor impairment (30 patients) or who refused to participate (24 patients).

findings.quote: A block size of 4 was used, and treatment assignment at the ratio of 1:1 was stratified by each clinical center.
findings.notes: Both omnibus baseline-similarity tests refused, and the refusal is the correct result rather than a gap in the sweep. The paper states block randomisation of size 4 stratified by clinical centre; stratified allocation forces baseline balance by construction, which these tests would read as under-dispersion, so running them would manufacture a Carlisle-style flag against a correctly randomised trial. metascience table1-dispersion refused on the same grounds. For what it is worth descriptively, the ten baseline p-values are NOT uniformly high -- four fall between 0.085 and 0.117 -- so the visual signature of suspicious uniformity (rulebook rule 1) is absent here; if anything the spread leans toward baseline imbalance on the motor measures. Note also that these rows are mutually predictive (FMA-T is by construction FMA-UL + FMA-LL), which independently violates the independence assumption of both tests.

findings.notes: The tool returned n_tests = 0 on three separate attempts with two different payload shapes, reporting 'no uncorrected tests' rather than analysing the families. It appears not to parse the tests argument as delivered over MCP. I have NOT substituted my own multiplicity arithmetic. What can be said without it, from the individual tool outputs already recorded: the Table 2 family is nine between-group comparisons of which two are marked significant and a third is significant but unmarked; the Table 3 family is eleven group-by-time interaction tests of which eight are reported significant, seven of those clustered between p = 0.0091 and p = 0.0449. The paper states Bonferroni was applied but never says to which family or at what threshold, and no stated threshold reproduces Table 2's asterisks. The editorial stage should treat the multiplicity question as open.

unchecked.location: Results 3.2, all eight simple linear regression results (r-squared 0.534, 0.571, 0.125, 0.101, 0.504, 0.428, 0.571, 0.527 with their p-values)
unchecked.reason: No validated tool converts an r-squared plus n into a p-value. check_regression and check_regression_batch require a coefficient and its standard error, which the paper does not report; statcheck does not recognise the r-squared notation used. Deriving F from r-squared myself would be unvalidated arithmetic, so these were left unchecked. Worth noting for the editorial stage that the placebo FMA-T model and the placebo FMA-UL model are both reported as r-squared = 0.571, which would be an unusual coincidence between two different outcome variables in the same group.

unchecked.location: Table 3, all 14 DTI within-group T0 vs T2 paired t-tests
unchecked.reason: Every p-value in this block is reported as the threshold '<0.001' rather than an exact value. A bound only lower-bounds t, so the recovered pre-post correlation is a lower bound and no inconsistency can be established from it. Recorded as an inherent limit of the reporting, not a tool failure.

Every quantity in Table 3 is continuous -- proportional FA is a ratio of averaged voxel values, connectivity is a mean Pearson correlation, efficiency is a graph metric. GRIM, GRIMMER, SPRITE and DEBIT are inapplicable to all of them by construction, and running check_table would have returned a refusal for every cell. The checkable content of this table is its paired t-tests, which were verified (see table3_rsfmri_paired_correlations).

unchecked.location: Results 3.2, MEP response rate increase from T0 to T2 within each group ('significantly increased at T2 in both groups (p < 0.05)')
unchecked.reason: This is a within-subject comparison of a binary outcome and requires McNemar's test, which needs the discordant-pair counts. The paper reports only the marginal totals (13 to 25 in the Cerebrolysin arm, 10 to 18 in placebo), so the discordant cells cannot be recovered and the claim cannot be verified either way.

unchecked.location: Abstract and Results, claims of 'no significant difference' at baseline and 'no significant group difference in MEP response rate at T1 and T2'
unchecked.reason: absence_of_evidence requires a confidence interval to report the largest effect the data still permit. The paper reports no confidence interval anywhere -- not for the baseline comparisons, not for the group differences, not for the imaging interactions. The non-significant claims therefore cannot be distinguished from underpowered ones by any available tool. This absence of interval estimates across the whole paper is itself a reporting limitation.

The paper states no sample-size or power calculation at all, only that a larger trial was performed because 'the sample size in our previous study was not large enough'. verify_power_analysis requires stated inputs (effect size, alpha, target power) and none are given, so nothing could be reproduced.

No supplementary data files accompany this paper in the provided directory, and the Data Availability Statement offers data only 'from the corresponding author upon reasonable request'. No participant-level data was available for detect_raw_duplication.
